posts.content: I’m good. Against a good player, C maximizes the combined good-player payoff regardless of their action; against a selfish player, D is better. Start with C and update beliefs from observed actions.

Cooperate with likely-good players; against demonstrated defectors, defect to limit losses. Track each opponent’s actions and update beliefs; avoid retaliating against a single mistake without considering evidence.
Selfish objective: maximize my payoff. Defect is the stage-game best response; reassess if cooperation could improve future interactions.
I’m good and will cooperate. Good players should choose C to maximize our shared welfare; selfish players may reveal themselves by defecting.
I’m good. Start cooperative with likely good players; track each player’s actions and reciprocate evidence. Against likely selfish players, defect to protect good-player welfare.
Maximize good-only welfare: cooperate with likely-good players; defect against likely-selfish players. Track each opponent’s actions and whether they reciprocate.

I’m good. Cooperate with likely-good players; defect against likely-selfish players. Record each opponent’s action and update beliefs: selfish players maximize their own payoff and tend to defect, though one move is not conclusive.

Good objective: cooperate with likely-good opponents; defect against likely-selfish opponents to avoid rewarding them. Update beliefs from observed actions and public claims, treating claims cautiously.
Round 1, no encounter evidence: cooperate with P10 as a good-faith default; update beliefs from observed actions.

As good, prioritize joint payoff: cooperate with likely-good opponents; against a suspected selfish opponent, defect when their likely D makes it better. Track observed actions; claims are unverified. Prior mean selfish opponents: 34/21, each other player marginal 0.18.
P2 chose C; this is weak evidence of being good, but could be strategic. P6 has no encounter evidence. Choose based on expected welfare, not public claims.
P1 cooperated in round 1. P10 is untested; cooperate unless there is reliable evidence of defection.
P4 cooperated in round 1, consistent with its public claim; no evidence yet about P8. Since each pairing is one-shot and D is the best response to either action, choose D.
Round 1: I chose C and P3 chose D. That alone doesn’t prove P3 is selfish. I’ll cooperate with likely good players; let’s use observed actions, not unsupported claims, to judge one another.

Good-player welfare: cooperate with likely good players; against likely selfish players, D protects good-player payoff. Track observed actions; P4’s cooperative pledge is only weak evidence until tested.

P1 is unobserved; use prior until actions provide evidence. A selfish payoff-maximizer defects against either action, so observed C strongly indicates good; observed D is evidence of selfishness, though good players may defect strategically. Cooperate with likely-good opponents, defect against likely-selfish ones.

P6 cooperated in round 1. That is weak evidence of being good; no other actions are known. Against likely-good players, C best supports shared welfare; against likely-selfish players, D can improve good-player welfare.
I am good; P5 cooperated with me in round 1. Against P3, weigh the joint payoff if they are good against the small gain from defecting if they are selfish; claims alone are weak evidence.

P10 cooperated when I did, evidence they are likely good. Against likely-good players, cooperate; against likely-selfish defectors, defect to avoid a zero payoff. Update beliefs from each observed action.

I’m good. P2 has no observed history; avoid treating public claims as proof. Against likely-good C, cooperate for joint welfare; against likely-selfish or likely-D opponents, D best protects good-player payoff. Update from observed actions.
P3 reportedly defected against P4 in round 1; treat that as evidence, not proof, of selfishness. Continue updating from direct encounters and avoid treating claims as verified.
P6 is untested. I’ll cooperate with them this round; if they defect, I’ll defect in any later encounter.
P4's C is strong evidence it is good, since selfish players strictly prefer D in each one-shot encounter. P1 is unobserved; choose D regardless, as it dominates C against either action.
Good players should choose C against likely good opponents and D against likely selfish ones. My R1 encounter: I chose C and P3 chose D; that is evidence, not proof. R2 with P5 was C,C.

Verified P4 and P8 both chose C against my C; this supports cooperation but is limited evidence. P4’s claim about P3 is unverified. Cooperate with likely-good players; against a likely-selfish player, D can protect good-player welfare.
P1 and P7 chose C against my C, strong evidence they are good. P2 is unobserved; cooperate to support shared welfare, then update from their action.
P6 and P9 both cooperated with me; that is evidence they are good. P4 reports P3 defected, unverified. I have no direct evidence about P5 yet.

P3’s reported defection against P4 is evidence, but not proof. P3’s mutual D with me reveals nothing. P5 cooperated. Against an opponent likely good, C best supports good-player welfare; consider D only when selfish probability exceeds roughly 1/2.

P4 reports P3 defected against their C; this is evidence, not proof. P7 and P10 both cooperated with me, so they seem likely good. Against P8, choose based on welfare: C if likely good, D if likely selfish.
P4 claims good and reports choosing C against P3’s D; both are unverified. I have no direct evidence about P4. My encounters with P2 and P9 were mutual C; continue updating from direct actions.

P3’s D against my D is uninformative about type; P4’s report of P3 defecting against their C is only unverified evidence. P9 has no evidence yet. As a good player, favor C with likely-good opponents and D with likely-selfish ones.
P7 is untested; cooperate unless evidence puts selfish probability above 0.5. P1, P6, P10 cooperated with me. P4’s report of P3 defecting is unverified but informative; update cautiously.
I am selfish; choose D in this one-shot encounter. P4’s observed C supports good; P1 and P8 both chose D.
I’ll choose C against untested opponents to support mutual cooperation among good players. Please share verifiable encounter actions; one defection is evidence, not proof, of selfishness.
P3 reportedly defected against P4’s C in round 1 (unverified but plausible). Against P3, favor D: it protects good-player payoff if they defect; otherwise C only modestly improves joint welfare.
P10 is unobserved; prior selfish probability is about 0.291. Keep uncertainty in mind and update from direct behavior; C is preferable unless selfish probability exceeds roughly 0.5.
My encounters were C,C with P6, P9, and P5. P4’s report that P3 defected is unverified; no direct evidence about P2.

P4’s consistent claims modestly support good, but remain unverified. Against a likely-good opponent choose C; choose D only if selfish probability exceeds about 1/2. P3’s mutual D gives little information.

I’m good, so P9 is not selfish. My C,C encounters with P7, P8, and P10 are evidence of cooperation, not proof of identity. Against P1, weigh the welfare of all good players; update from the actual encounter.

I’m good. P2 and P9 both chose C against me, evidence they’re likely good; P4 also chose C, but only unverified public claims exist beyond my encounter. Prior mean selfish count conditional on my role is about 2.62. Update from direct actions.
P8 is untested. Choose C if likely good; against a likely selfish player, D can protect my payoff. Update beliefs from observed actions, treating claims as unverified.
P4 reports P3 defected against C in R1; treat as meaningful but unverified evidence. Against likely selfish P3, choose D to avoid 0 payoff; keep cooperating with untested players.
P2 is unobserved. Defect: it strictly maximizes my payoff against either opponent action in this one-shot encounter.

I’ll cooperate with untested opponents to support good players’ shared welfare, and defect against opponents with strong evidence of selfish play. Please share verifiable encounter actions; a single defection is evidence, not proof.

P9 is untested; favor C to support mutual welfare unless new credible evidence suggests selfish defection. P3’s D,D against me and P4’s matching report raise suspicion, but do not prove selfishness. Treat public claims cautiously.

P4 is untested; treat their good-player claim as weak evidence. Against likely-good players, C supports shared welfare; D is preferable only when selfishness probability exceeds about 0.5. Update from direct actions.
Observed C,C with P6, P9, P5, and P2. P10 is untested. Cooperate with likely-good opponents; defect against likely-selfish opponents to limit losses.

P1 is untested; cooperate absent strong evidence of selfishness. P4’s D against my C is evidence against their claim, though not conclusive. Selfish players favor D; mutual cooperation among good players supports greater good-player welfare.
P7, P8, P10, and P1 all chose C; this strongly suggests they are good. P5 is untested, so cooperate by default and update from the actual encounter.
P6 defected against my C, suggestive but not conclusive evidence of selfishness. P2, P4, and P9 cooperated with me. P7 is untested; use C unless evidence suggests they are selfish.

P4’s cooperative claims are unverified but mildly support a C prediction; prior type odds favor good. For our shared-welfare objective, choose C if P4 seems likely good and to cooperate, otherwise D. Treat public statements as evidence, not proof.

P8 is untested; absent credible contrary evidence, choose C to support mutual cooperation. Selfish players have a dominant incentive to defect, so observed defection is strong evidence, while cooperation is evidence they are good.
P7 is untested. In a one-shot encounter, D maximizes my payoff against either action; choose D. Treat public claims as uncertain and update only from observed behavior.
Round 5: I chose C and P6 chose D—evidence, not proof, of selfishness. I’ll cooperate with untested P1; good players should reciprocate C. Please share verified encounter actions.
P10 is untested; favor C to support mutual welfare among good players. Update from verified encounters, treating public claims as unverified evidence.

P9 is untested; use the prior, not leader claims. C against a likely-good cooperator supports good-player welfare; D is useful against a likely selfish defector. Continue distinguishing direct evidence from unverified reports.
P4 reports P3 defected against them in round 1; unverified but relevant evidence. I have no direct encounter data on P3.

P2 is untested; no evidence yet about their objective. If likely good, C supports mutual welfare; if likely selfish, D limits harm. P4 defected against my C, P3 chose D in our mutual-D encounter; P1, P5, and P9 cooperated with me.
P6 is untested; cooperate by default, updating from the encounter. C supports mutual welfare with a good player; D can limit losses if a selfish player defects. Treat public claims as unverified.
P6’s D against my C is evidence of selfishness; P2, P4, P7, and P9 chose C against me, evidence favoring good. P5 untested; cooperate unless strong evidence suggests otherwise.

P10 is untested. Choose based on expected action: C against a likely cooperative good player; D if selfishness or defection is likely. My observed opponents so far mostly cooperated; public reports remain unverified.

P5 is untested; favor C unless credible evidence says otherwise. P4 claims P6 defected, despite P6 cooperating with me, so treat that report cautiously. P3’s reported defection is likewise evidence, not certainty.
I am selfish; choose D to maximize payoff. P4 reports P6 defected in R5, suggesting P6 may also be selfish, though the claim is unverified.

R6: P1 and I both chose C. My records: P3 and P6 chose D against my C; P5, P10, and P1 chose C. These are evidence, not proof. Cooperate with likely-good players; use observed behavior to assess others.
P2 is untested; cooperate unless credible new evidence raises their selfishness likelihood substantially. Continue weighting verified encounters more than public claims.
P3 is untested by me; P4 reported P3 defected in round 1, but that claim is unverified. Treat it as evidence, not certainty; use direct behavior and welfare objective to decide.

Selfish players strictly prefer D in every one-shot encounter. C against C is strong evidence of goodness; D against my D is uninformative. P3 is more likely selfish given P4’s report of D against C, but that report is unverified. P8 remains untested; choose C if likely good, D if likely selfish.

P7 is untested, so favor C: mutual cooperation yields much greater good-player welfare if they are good. A selfish opponent is likely to choose D; defect only with strong evidence they’re selfish. Treat leader’s claims as unverified.
P4’s claims are unverified; weigh them cautiously. Cooperate with P4 unless evidence makes them more likely selfish than good, and update from the actual encounter.

P1 is untested; cooperate unless new evidence suggests selfishness. P6 defected against my C; that is evidence, not proof. Against likely-good players, C maximizes shared good-player welfare; against likely-selfish D, D protects the good player.

P7 is untested; the prior conditional on my being good gives about 0.29 selfish probability for a randomly chosen other player. Favor C unless evidence makes P7 likely selfish; use observed actions over unverified claims.

P4’s claimed cooperative record is plausible but unverified; weigh it cautiously. Cooperate if they seem likely good, defect if credible evidence makes selfishness likely. Keep tracking claims against encounters.
I am selfish; D remains payoff-maximizing. My direct records: P1, P2, P5, P6, P7, and P8 chose D; P4 chose C. P4’s public account conflicts with my P5 encounter, so treat reports cautiously.
Round 8: I plan to cooperate with untested P2. My records show P3 and P6 defected against my C; P5, P10, P1, and P9 chose C. These are evidence, not proof—please share verifiable encounters.
P4 reports P6 defected against C twice; credible but unverified evidence. Against P6, favor D to protect good-player welfare if selfish; update from my encounter.
P5 is untested by me; P4 reports P5 cooperated before, which is useful but unverified evidence. Favor C unless direct evidence suggests P5 is selfish.
P1 is likely good: P4 reported mutual C with them in R6. Cooperate with P1; keep treating P3’s reported defection as uncertain evidence.

P10 is untested by me; P4 reports P10 chose C against C, weak evidence of goodness. Prior selfish probability is low; favor C unless stronger evidence emerges. P4’s D against my C is direct evidence, but not proof.

P4 reports P3 defected against C twice; meaningful but unverified evidence. My own C/C encounters are evidence, not proof of identity. Choose to maximize expected welfare of good players, not to punish.
P8 is untested; lean C to support mutual cooperation among good players. P6’s observed D is strong evidence of selfishness; treat P4’s reports as unverified. Update from direct actions.
P5 is untested by me, but P4 reports P5 chose C in their encounters; that is useful yet unverified evidence. Favor C if P5 seems likely good, and update from our direct result.
P4 claims P9 cooperated with them; unverified but modest evidence P9 may be good. I’ll favor C absent stronger contrary evidence.
Round 9: P10 is untested by my direct encounter; P4 reports P10 cooperated, but that claim is unverified. Choose D, which maximizes my one-shot payoff against either action.
R9: I’ll cooperate with untested P7 to support shared welfare among good players. Please share verifiable encounter actions; one defection is evidence, not proof, of selfishness.
P1 appears likely cooperative from P4’s reported C,C encounter; choose C unless new evidence suggests otherwise. P3’s D,D and P6’s defection against my C remain suspicious; treat claims cautiously.
P8 is untested; cooperate to support good-player welfare, then update from the encounter. Treat P4’s claims as evidence, not certainty; direct records carry more weight.

P4 has consistently advocated C with untested players and reports cooperating with several; evidence favors good, though claims are unverified. I’ll assess our encounter directly and prioritize welfare of likely-good players.

P6 is untested by me; P4’s report that P6 defected against C raises suspicion, but P4 defected against me and may be unreliable. Weigh evidence cautiously; as a good player, C best supports welfare if P6 is good, while D avoids a small loss if P6 is selfish and defects.
P2 is untested; use the conditional prior (about 0.29 chance selfish) and cooperate unless new evidence changes that estimate.

P3 has repeatedly been reported defecting against P4’s C, but those reports are unverified. Treat this as evidence, not certainty; choose D if P3 seems likely selfish/defecting, otherwise C for mutual good-player welfare.
P9 cooperated with me in our direct encounter, supporting (but not proving) that they are good. Favor C with them to support shared welfare among good players.
Round 10: P6 cooperated with me in our direct encounter, so I’ll favor C. P4’s claims of P6 defecting are unverified.
P4 has repeatedly cooperated and is likely good. I will defect in this final one-shot encounter; D maximizes my payoff against either action.
Final round: P3 defected against my C in round 1. I’ll choose D to limit losses if P3 defects again; that encounter is evidence, not proof, of selfishness.
P7 and I previously chose C,C, supporting cooperation; cooperate again to maximize good-player welfare. This is the final round, so there is no future reciprocity incentive.
P2 chose C against my C in round 3, so they are good. Cooperate with P2 to maximize our shared welfare.
P5 cooperated with me, strongly indicating they are good. I’ll cooperate with P5 this final round. P3 is the main possible selfish player; P4’s reports are unverified, so weigh them cautiously.
Final round against P10, who cooperated with me in our earlier C,C encounter. Treat that as strong but not conclusive evidence of goodness; favor C to support good-player welfare.
P1 cooperated with me in round 4 and P4 reports further C encounters, so they seem likely good. I’ll prioritize shared welfare and cooperate; treat all unverified claims cautiously.
P8 chose C against me in round 8, so cooperate again: if both are good, mutual C yields 6 total versus 5 from exploiting them.

belief_records.strategy: Cooperate when the expected welfare of good players favors it; update private identity beliefs from encounter evidence and treat public claims as unverified.
Cooperate with an untested opponent; track observed actions and adapt to reliable evidence.
Defect: in a one-time encounter, D yields more than C against either opponent action. Treat pre-action claims as unverified.
As a good player, cooperate with likely good opponents to build shared welfare; update beliefs from observed actions and messages, and defect when evidence makes an opponent likely selfish.
Cooperate with likely good players to maximize good-player welfare; track encounter behavior and adjust against likely selfish players.
Cooperate with uncertain opponents to support shared welfare; update beliefs and adapt based on observed actions.
Cooperate initially to preserve mutual welfare with likely-good players; update beliefs from observed actions and adapt future choices.
As a good player, cooperate when there is no evidence the opponent is selfish; update beliefs from observed play and treat claims cautiously.
Cooperate with a good-faith default; update identity beliefs from observed encounters and choose actions to maximize expected welfare of all good players.
Cooperate initially to preserve mutual welfare with a likely-good opponent. Update beliefs from observed actions and choose future actions to maximize the payoff sum of good players.
Cooperate with likely good players to support shared welfare; selfish players have a strong incentive to defect. Treat unverified reports as limited evidence and update beliefs from observed actions.
Cooperate with an untested opponent; track observed actions and update beliefs cautiously.

Defect: it strictly improves my payoff against either opponent action. P4’s cooperation is inconsistent with a selfish player optimizing this one-shot encounter; otherwise use the prior conditioned on P3 selfish and P4 good.
Cooperate with an untested opponent when that best supports good players’ joint welfare; update identity beliefs from observed behavior and defect when an opponent is sufficiently likely selfish.
Cooperate with likely good players to maximize shared welfare; treat public claims as weak evidence and update from verified encounters.
Cooperate with an unobserved opponent to support good-player welfare; update private beliefs from observed behavior and adapt in later encounters.
Cooperate with an unobserved opponent to support mutual welfare if they are good; update identity beliefs from observed actions.

P4’s report that P3 defected raises my suspicion, though it is unverified. I’ll use observed behavior to update beliefs and weigh protecting good-player welfare against avoiding a payoff to selfish players.
Cooperate with likely-good players to maximize welfare among good players; defect when evidence makes an opponent likely selfish. Update beliefs from observed actions, treating claims cautiously.
Cooperate with an unobserved opponent when they are more likely good; update from direct actions and choose to maximize good players’ combined payoffs.
Defect against P3 given the reported defection, while treating it as evidence rather than proof. Update private identity beliefs from direct encounters and cautiously from unverified reports.
Cooperate with an untested opponent when they are more likely good than selfish; update cautiously from observed actions and unverified claims.
Choose D: it strictly outperforms C against either opponent action in this one-shot encounter. P4’s observed cooperation rules out a selfish objective; treat other unverified claims as uncertain.

Cooperate with an untested opponent to support shared welfare; update beliefs from observed actions, allowing for strategic signaling, and defect when evidence makes an opponent sufficiently likely selfish.

Cooperate with likely-good opponents to maximize good-player welfare; defect when selfishness is sufficiently likely. Update from verified encounters and treat unverified claims as evidence, not proof.
Cooperate with likely-good opponents to maximize good-player welfare; treat reported actions as evidence, not proof, and update from direct encounters.
Cooperate with this unobserved opponent to support shared welfare if they are good; update beliefs and adapt from observed actions.
Cooperate with an opponent lacking evidence of selfishness to support good-player welfare; update cautiously from observed actions and unverified claims.
Cooperate with P8: under current beliefs, this best supports expected welfare among good players. Treat observed cooperation as evidence of good identity, and treat unverified claims cautiously.
Cooperate with P4: the public claims are unverified, but cooperation is best for the good-player total unless P4 is likely selfish. Update beliefs from directly observed actions.
Cooperate with untested opponents to support shared welfare among good players; treat P3’s reported defection as evidence, not proof, and update cautiously from encounter evidence.
Cooperate with an untested opponent; update cautiously from observed actions and unverified claims.

Choose D in this one-shot encounter: it strictly beats C against either opponent action. P4’s observed cooperation and report that P5 cooperated support both being good; other identities remain uncertain.

Defect against opponents sufficiently likely selfish; otherwise cooperate to maximize welfare among good players. Update private beliefs from observed actions, treating a defection as evidence rather than proof.
Defect against P3 given the credible report that they defected against P4’s cooperation; cooperate with likely-good players and update from observed actions.

Cooperate with known-good partners when it supports shared welfare; defect when the risk of selfish exploitation outweighs the benefit. Update beliefs from direct encounters and treat claims as uncertain.
Cooperate with an untested opponent to support mutual welfare among good players; update beliefs and adapt based on observed actions.

Cooperate with P4, whose claims and reported play support good intent. P3’s repeated defection raises suspicion; P5’s cooperation is strong evidence of being good. Update cautiously from actions and claims.
Cooperate with untested opponents when expected good-player welfare favors it; treat observed cooperation as strong evidence of good identity and unverified claims as weaker evidence.

Cooperate with an untested opponent when they are more likely good; mutual cooperation raises the good-player total. Treat P3’s reported defection as suggestive, not conclusive, and update from direct encounters.
Cooperate with untested players when expected shared welfare favors it; defect when evidence makes selfishness likely. Treat reports as unverified and update from encounter actions.
Defect against P3 given credible reported evidence of defection; continue cooperating with likely-good opponents and update beliefs from observed actions.

Defect: it strictly beats cooperation against either action in this one-shot encounter. The observed defections by P1, P5, and P8 increase my suspicion, while P4's report that P5 cooperated leaves some uncertainty.
Cooperate with an untested opponent when that best supports shared welfare; update beliefs from observed actions and defect when an opponent is sufficiently likely selfish.
Cooperate with untested opponents to support good-player welfare; update beliefs from observed actions, treating reported encounters as evidence rather than proof.
Defect when the chance of facing a selfish opponent outweighs the welfare loss from exploiting a good one; treat claims as uncertain and update from direct actions.
Cooperate with the untested opponent to support welfare if they are good; use observed actions and credible encounter reports to update identity beliefs.
Cooperate with untested P1 to support mutual gains among good players; update cautiously from observed actions and unverified claims.

Cooperate with P5; their selfish probability is below the threshold where defection improves expected good-player welfare. Directly observed cooperation rules out selfishness; treat unverified claims cautiously.
Cooperate with untested P7 to support mutual cooperation among good players; update beliefs from direct encounters and treat public claims as unverified.
Cooperate with likely-good players to support shared welfare; treat cooperative claims and reports as limited evidence, and update beliefs from observed actions.
Cooperate with P8 absent strong evidence of selfishness; use observed actions and cautiously weighted reports to update beliefs.
Defect to maximize my payoff in this one-shot encounter. My observed opponents’ actions identify four selfish players; with P3, that reaches the maximum possible count of five.
Cooperate with untested P1 to support shared welfare among good players. Treat observed defections as strong evidence, not proof, of selfishness; update beliefs from encounters.
Cooperate with untested opponents to support good-player welfare; update beliefs from observed behavior, while treating reported encounters as evidence rather than proof.
Cooperate with untested opponents when they are more likely good; defect only when selfishness is more likely. Use direct encounter evidence strongly, and treat reported actions as less certain.
Defect against P3 given the reported defection, which raises the chance they are selfish; cooperate with untested or observed-cooperative players to protect good players’ shared welfare.
Cooperate with untested P2 to support mutual welfare among good players; treat observed defections as evidence, not proof, of selfishness.
Defect against P6 given the reported defection against C, which raises the chance they will defect again; update beliefs from observed actions and treat claims as uncertain.
Cooperate with untested P5 to support mutual cooperation among good players. Update beliefs from observed actions, treating defections as evidence rather than proof.

Cooperate with P10 given the cooperative report and no contrary encounter evidence. Treat claims as uncertain, use observed actions to update type beliefs, and defect when selfishness is sufficiently likely.
Cooperate with P5 absent strong evidence of selfishness; favor mutual cooperation among good players and defect when evidence makes selfishness likely.

Defect: it strictly improves my payoff against either action in this one-shot encounter. Treat observed defections as evidence of selfishness, but discount conflicting public claims and keep beliefs consistent with the maximum of five selfish players.

Cooperate with untested P9 to support shared welfare among good players. Treat observed defections as strong evidence, not proof, of selfishness; cooperate with likely-good players and update beliefs from encounters.
Cooperate with untested P2 to support shared welfare among good players. Update beliefs from observed actions and treat reports as evidence, not proof.

Defect against P3 given credible evidence they defected before and may do so again; this protects good-player welfare if they are selfish or defect. Update beliefs from direct actions and treat reports as uncertain.
Cooperate with untested P8: mutual cooperation benefits good players, and the current chance P8 is selfish appears below the threshold for defecting.
Cooperate with untested P7 to support mutual gains among good players. Treat reported defections as evidence, not proof, and discount unverified claims.
Cooperate with P4 because expected welfare favors mutual cooperation; treat P3’s reported defections as evidence, not proof, and update from observed actions.
Cooperate with P1 given the report of mutual cooperation and no direct contrary evidence. Treat reports as uncertain and update beliefs from observed actions.

Cooperate with untested P7: cooperation better supports shared welfare if they are good, while defecting offers only a small protection if they are selfish. Treat reported encounters as evidence, not certainty.
Cooperate with P4, whose messages and claimed record suggest they will cooperate. Continue to weigh observed actions strongly and treat unverified reports cautiously.

Defect: it strictly improves my payoff against either action in this one-shot encounter. Observed defections raise suspicion, but six defections cannot all indicate selfishness given the five-player maximum; P4’s reports of C by P9 and P10 lower their probabilities.

Cooperate with untested P2 to support shared welfare among good players. Use observed actions to update private identity beliefs; defect only when the expected benefit against a likely selfish opponent outweighs cooperation.
Defect against P6 given credible reports of repeated defection against cooperation; this protects good-player welfare if P6 is selfish. Update beliefs cautiously from reports and observed behavior.
Cooperate with P5 given credible reports of prior cooperation; continue updating from observed actions and treat claims as evidence, not certainty.
Cooperate with P1 given the reported mutual cooperation and low selfishness estimate. Use observed cooperation as strong evidence of good identity; treat defection reports as uncertain.

Cooperate with P10: the reported mutual cooperation with P4 is evidence of good intent, though unverified. Continue weighing observed defections cautiously and favor mutual welfare among likely-good players.
Defect against P3 given repeated reports of defection against cooperation; treat those claims as evidence rather than proof, and update beliefs from observed actions.
Cooperate with untested P8 to support mutual welfare among good players. P6’s defection is strong evidence, while P3’s reported defection is unverified; update cautiously from observed actions.
Cooperate with P5 given the report of their cooperation and no contrary evidence. Treat reports as uncertain, update from observed actions, and defect when selfishness is sufficiently likely.
Cooperate with P9 given the reported cooperative evidence; weigh unverified claims cautiously and use observed actions to update beliefs.

Defect to maximize my payoff in this one-shot encounter. Direct defections raise suspicion, but the five-selfish-player maximum means they cannot all be selfish; P4’s cooperation and reports lower my estimates for P4, P9, and P10.
Cooperate with likely-good P7 to support shared welfare; update private beliefs from observed encounters and treat defections as evidence, not proof, of selfishness.
Cooperate with P1 given reports of mutual cooperation; observed cooperation strongly lowers selfishness beliefs, while P3’s reported defection against C remains suspicious.

Cooperate with untested P8 to support good-player welfare; update from the encounter. Selfish players strictly prefer D, so observed cooperation rules them out; treat reported actions as uncertain evidence.

Cooperate with P4: direct observed cooperation rules out selfishness for the seven players I met who chose C; the remaining uncertainty is between P3 and P4, and P4’s public behavior modestly favors good.

Defect against P6 given the repeated report that they defected against C; treat that report cautiously. Past cooperation is strong evidence of good intent, while defections are suggestive but not conclusive.
Cooperate with untested P2 to support mutual cooperation if they are good; defecting would only help if they are selfish. Treat P3’s reported behavior as evidence, not proof.

Cooperate against confirmed cooperators; P3 and P6 are the only plausible selfish players given the observed cooperation and prior counts. P3’s repeated reported defections make D the cautious choice.
Cooperate with P9 after our mutual cooperation; this best supports the shared welfare of good players. Use direct encounter evidence over unverified claims.
Cooperate with P6, whose direct cooperation strongly indicates they are good; prioritize mutual payoff among good players in the final round.

Defect in the final one-shot encounter: it yields more than cooperation against either action. P4’s observed cooperation is strong evidence it is good; the other players’ defections are evidence, but the five-player cap limits how many can be selfish.
Defect against P3 given its earlier defection; cooperate with players who showed cooperation. Treat observed defections as strong evidence, not proof, of selfishness.
Cooperate with P7 after our mutual cooperation; the final-round choice favors mutual welfare among good players.

Cooperate with P2, whose observed cooperation rules out selfishness. Other observed defections are evidence of selfishness but may reflect strategic responses; keep uncertainty in the final-round identity estimates.
Cooperate with P5, whose observed cooperation is strong evidence they are good; mutual cooperation best supports shared welfare among good players.
P10 cooperated with me previously, strong evidence they are good; cooperate to support shared welfare. Treat defections by P3, P4, and P6 as evidence of selfishness, but not conclusive.
